record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.original_question: For sample-splitting methods in observational study protocols, how can sequential analysis methods be used to allow multiple possible planning samples before researchers decide on the final analysis sample for confirmatory testing?

evidence.quote: Examples of methods that control for the familywise multiple testing error rate are Bonferroni-Holm [56] or splitting in which the data is randomly divided into a planning sample and an analysis sample, hypotheses are chosen to test based on examining the planning sample and then the chosen hypotheses are tested on the analysis sample using Bonferroni-Holm with the number of hypotheses now being the number of chosen hypotheses from the planning sample [25, 117, 47].

In Section 5, we demonstrated that splitting may be a useful approach for selecting outcomes and subgroups in an observational study. Some problems that have not been well explored for the approach include (i) what is a good fraction for the planning sample based on the sample size?; (ii) how should we decide how many and which outcomes should be carried forward from the planning sample to test in the analysis sample?; and (iii) instead of just having one planning sample and one analysis sample, how can we use sequential analysis methods to allow for multiple possible planning samples before deciding on an analysis sample?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the following setup for confirmatory hypothesis testing in an observational study. A data set of n independent units is available, on which a researcher wishes to test some unspecified family of null hypotheses concerning the effect of a treatment on possibly multiple outcomes and/or in possibly multiple subgroups. In the classical "single-split" protocol, one randomly partitions the n units into a planning sample of size n_P and an analysis sample of size n_A = n - n_P. The planning sample is examined freely to choose a subset S of hypotheses to carry forward; these hypotheses are then tested in the analysis sample, controlling the familywise error rate at level alpha using a Bonferroni–Holm correction in which the number of hypotheses equals |S|. Because the planning and analysis samples are independent, this procedure controls the familywise error rate at level alpha regardless of how S is chosen.

Develop and analyze a sequential generalization of this protocol that allows multiple successive planning stages before the final analysis sample is fixed. Formally, design a procedure of the following type:

- Specify a sequence of disjoint subsamples D_1, D_2, ..., D_K, D_A of the data, where each D_k serves as a tentative "planning sample" used to refine the candidate hypothesis set H_k ⊆ H_{k-1}, and D_A is the eventual analysis sample.
- Allow a data-dependent stopping rule τ ∈ {1, ..., K} (a stopping time with respect to the filtration generated by D_1, ..., D_τ) at which the researcher commits to a final hypothesis set H_τ and tests these hypotheses on D_A.
- Provide a multiple-testing adjustment such that the resulting protocol controls the familywise error rate at level alpha, uniformly over all admissible stopping rules and selection rules.

Specifically, the problem is to:

(a) Give an explicit construction of such a sequential planning/analysis splitting scheme together with a valid multiple-testing correction.
(b) Prove finite-sample familywise error rate control at level alpha for the proposed procedure.
(c) Characterize, under reasonable models for treatment effects and unmeasured bias (e.g., a Rosenbaum sensitivity-analysis Γ-model), how the choice of K, the sizes |D_k| and |D_A|, and the stopping rule affect statistical power compared to the single-split protocol, and identify conditions under which the sequential scheme strictly dominates a single split.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., "Planning for gold" 2024, "Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies" 2026) addresses the choice of split fraction and which hypotheses to carry forward, and cross-screening / data-turnover frameworks split the data into two planning halves. However, a general sequential-analysis extension allowing multiple successive planning samples with a data-dependent stopping rule before fixing the analysis sample, together with a corresponding familywise-error-controlling multiple-testing adjustment and power analysis, does not appear to have been carried out in the literature; it is described as an unexplored direction.

status_evidence.title: Planning for gold: Hypothesis screening with split samples
status_evidence.snippet: Splitting the data into a planning sample for choosing the design and an analysis sample for making inferences; the choice of split fraction is studied via plasmode datasets.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work addresses split-fraction and hypothesis-selection questions for single-split protocols but not the sequential multi-planning-sample extension.

status_evidence.title: Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies
status_evidence.snippet: Develops optimal sample splitting fractions for observational study design, focused on a single planning/analysis split.
status_evidence.claim: Optimal split fraction is studied, but sequential generalizations are not the focus.

status_evidence.title: Split-Sample Strategies for Avoiding False Discoveries
status_evidence.snippet: Cross-screening splits data in half, uses each half to plan and analyze the other, adjusting with Bonferroni.
status_evidence.claim: Cross-screening extends single splitting to two halves but is not a fully sequential procedure with multiple planning samples and a stopping rule.
